desc: The second and more consequential official Air Force report, authored by James McAndrew and published by Headquarters United States Air Force through the Government Printing Office in 1997, addressing the alien-bodies claims that the 1994-1995 report had not covered. Its four stated conclusions are that Air Force activities spanning many years were consolidated into two or three days in July 1947; that the 'aliens' were probably anthropomorphic test dummies carried aloft by high-altitude balloons; that the 'unusual' military activity in the desert was balloon launch and recovery, with the units that always arrived shortly after a crash being accurate descriptions of dummy-recovery teams; and that the Roswell Army Air Field hospital bodies claims most likely combine a 1956 KC-97 crash killing eleven airmen with a 1959 manned balloon mishap injuring two pilots. The report also asserts flatly that 'the claims of bodies only became part of the Roswell Incident after 1978'. What makes it a first-order artifact rather than a press release is what it printed: anthropomorphic dummy launch and landing locations at Appendix A; sworn witness statements from ten named Air Force personnel at Appendix B including Col. Joseph W. Kittinger Jr., Col. Dan D. Fulgham, Bernard D. Gildenberg and Lt. Col. Raymond A. Madson; and full interview transcripts of five pro-UFO witnesses at Appendix C - Gerald Anderson, Glenn Dennis, Alice Knight, Vern Maltais and James Ragsdale, the Dennis interview supplied by its interviewer Karl T. Pflock. Section 2.1 is the most forensically detailed passage the US government has ever published on a UFO claim: it works the 427th AAF Base Unit Squadron 'M' morning reports and the National Personnel Records Center holdings to establish that Glenn Dennis's 'Naomi Maria Selff' never existed and to identify 1st Lt. Eileen M. Fanton as matching every other particular of his description.

dossier.denialPosture: This document is the denial. It asserts finality in its title, expressly rejects "allegations that the Air Force has engaged in a cover-up," and explains every witness-reported element of a retrieval operation as a misdated observation of an unclassified Air Force program. It is a denial of interpretation rather than of events, which is a distinct and more durable rhetorical form.
dossier.narrative:
The sequence matters more than the content. In 1993 Rep. Steven H. Schiff (R-New Mexico) began asking the Department of Defense about Roswell and, dissatisfied, referred the matter to the General Accounting Office. The GAO tasking forced the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force into an exhaustive records search that concluded in July 1994 and produced roughly 1,000 pages of material, published in 1995 as The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert. Secretary of the Air Force Sheila E. Widnall released interviewees from any security obligations that might have restricted their statements. The 1995 report's answer was Project Mogul: a then-classified balloon-borne acoustic sensor program whose train components, it said, accounted for the debris. Notably, the Mogul records that carried the explanatory weight had never been classified at all; other Mogul records had been declassified en masse under Executive Order 11652, signed by President Nixon on 6 March 1972.

Mogul explained debris. It did not explain bodies. Case Closed exists to close that gap, and its four stated conclusions are worth reading as a list of the specific narrative threads the Air Force needed cut. First, that Air Force activities occurring over a period of many years "have been consolidated and are now represented to have occurred in two or three days in July 1947." Second, that "'Aliens' observed in the New Mexico desert were probably anthropomorphic test dummies that were carried aloft by U.S. Air Force high altitude balloons for scientific research." Third, that the reports of military units arriving shortly after a crash to retrieve a saucer and its crew "were actually accurate descriptions of Air Force personnel engaged in anthropomorphic dummy recovery operations." Fourth, that claims of bodies at the Roswell Army Air Field hospital were most likely a conflation of a 1956 KC-97 accident in which eleven airmen were killed and a 1959 manned balloon mishap in which two pilots were injured.

Read as an intelligence product, this is a substitution table. Each item on the left is a witness-reported element of a retrieval operation - non-human bodies, a cordon, a convoy, a hospital, injured or dead personnel - and each item on the right is a real, documented, unclassified Air Force activity that produces the same observable. The Air Force is not arguing that nothing happened. It is arguing that everything happened, repeatedly, over fifteen years, and that the witnesses stacked it. The named substitutes are Projects High Dive and Excelsior, the Holloman-based dummy-drop and high-altitude-bailout programs; the dummies are identified in the report's own figures as Alderson Laboratories and 'Sierra Sam' type anthropomorphic dummies. Appendix B is a set of signed sworn statements from in-person interviews, including Col. Charles A. Coltman Jr. (USAF Medical Corps, retired), Col. Dan D. Fulgham (retired) - the pilot injured in the 1959 balloon mishap - and Bernard D. Gildenberg, the Holloman balloon engineer.

The report's own framing gives away its function. It states that its findings run "Contrary to allegations that the Air Force has engaged in a cover-up and possesses dark secrets involving the Roswell claims." That sentence is not a finding; it is a rebuttal, and it identifies the audience. The title itself - Case Closed - is a declaration of jurisdiction over when an inquiry ends, which is the specific authority a service branch does not actually have with respect to Congress.

What the report does not address is the record-destruction finding that emerged from the same GAO audit. GAO/NSIAD-95-187, released 28 July 1995, reported that RAAF administrative records from March 1945 through December 1949 and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, and that the document disposition form did not indicate what organization or person destroyed them, when, or under what authority. The GAO also found that Army Air Force regulations in 1947 required air accident reports to be maintained permanently, that four such accidents were reported in New Mexico in July 1947 - all after 8 July, the date the RAAF public information office announced recovery of a flying disc - and that USAF officials told GAO there was no requirement to report the crash of a balloon.

Case Closed has since been absorbed into the current official narrative without qualification. AARO's Historical Record Report Volume 1, published 8 March 2024, cites it approvingly, restating the dummy explanation and the 1956/1959 hospital conflation verbatim as established results. That continuity is the point: the 1997 denial is not a historical curiosity, it is a live load-bearing element of the 2024 denial.

dossier.whatItIs: The Roswell Report: Case Closed is a 231-page official United States Air Force publication authored by Capt. James McAndrew of the Secretary of the Air Force Declassification and Review Team at the Pentagon, printed by the U.S. Government Printing Office and released on 24 June 1997. It is the follow-on to the 1994-95 Air Force report The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert by Col. Richard L. Weaver and then-1st Lt. James McAndrew. Its purpose is to account for the reports of 'alien bodies' that the 1995 report had left unaddressed.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is a denial artifact, and it is catalogued here as evidence about the denier rather than about Roswell. It is dated, signed, congressionally provoked, and printed at government expense, which makes it the most attributable statement the Air Force has ever made on the subject - and its internal logic reveals precisely which claims the Air Force judged it could not leave standing. Its core mechanism is temporal: it asserts that Air Force activities spread across many years have been consolidated by witnesses into two or three days in July 1947, and that UFO proponents mis-dated the 'alien' observations "in some instances by more than a decade." It was released on the 50th anniversary of the Kenneth Arnold sighting, a date choice that is itself a communications decision. And it is the direct product of a General Accounting Office audit initiated at the request of a sitting member of Congress, which means the Air Force wrote it under external compulsion rather than voluntarily - the only such instance in the pre-2017 record. The GAO audit that produced it also established, on the record, that Roswell Army Air Field's administrative records for March 1945 through December 1949 and its outgoing messages for October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, with no indication of by whom or under what authority.

entityInfo.desc: The most heavily documented artifact in the Roswell record, on either side. It prints the anthropomorphic dummy launch and landing locations, sworn statements from ten named Air Force personnel including Joseph W. Kittinger Jr., and full interview transcripts of the five principal pro-UFO witnesses. Its Section 2.1 nurse analysis is the only occasion on which the United States government has publicly worked a UFO witness claim down to certified daily personnel accounting records and named the individual it believes the witness actually described. Whatever one concludes about Project Mogul and the dummies, this is the standard of documentation this board holds every claim to, including the ones it finds persuasive.
